docs.title: Introduction to Scratch
docs.text:
Scratch is a visual programming tool that lets you create games, animations, stories, and interactive projects. Instead of typing code, you build programs by joining blocks together. This makes it easier to focus on how a program works, how instructions fit together, and how to solve problems step by step.

We use Scratch because it helps you learn important programming ideas in a clear and practical way. You can see your code running straight away, test your ideas quickly, and improve your project as you go.

docs.title: What Scratch helps us learn
docs.text:
Scratch helps us practise:

  • Giving clear instructions to a computer.
  • Breaking a problem into smaller steps.
  • Using events to make something happen.
  • Using loops to repeat actions.
  • Using conditions to make decisions.
  • Using variables to store and change information.
  • Testing, debugging, and improving a program.
  • Designing projects that people can use, play, or interact with.

docs.title: Why these skills matter
docs.text:
Programming is not just about making something work. It is about thinking carefully, solving problems, testing ideas, and learning from mistakes. Scratch gives you a safe place to practise these skills while creating something of your own.

As you work through the projects, you will become more confident at planning, building, testing, and improving digital solutions.

docs.title: Scratch Arcade Quest
docs.text: Build a platform game where your player jumps, collects collectables, dodges enemies, and reaches a finish flag.

docs.title: Get Started
docs.text:
1. Open Scratch desktop.
  2. Create a new project called Arcade Quest.
  3. Use Next in the navigation at the bottom of this page to open Draw Your Player. You will make the sprites and scenery as you work through the tasks.

Work at your own pace

The project has nine parts. A part may take more than one class session. Complete and check each task before moving on. If you have already started, carry on from your last task using the navigation.

docs.title: Experiences and Outcomes
docs.text:
Arcade Quest helps you work towards the following Curriculum for Excellence Computing Science Level 3 standards.

Experience and Outcome Level 3 benchmark What you will do in Arcade Quest Evidence of success TCH 3-13a — I can describe different fundamental information processes and how they communicate and can identify their use in solving different problems. Explains the difference between parallel processes and those that communicate with each other. Run scripts for the player, collectables, enemy, timer, flag, and Stage at the same time. Use broadcasts such as ouch, game over, and you win so these processes communicate. You can explain which scripts run independently and how a broadcast changes what another sprite or the Stage does. TCH 3-14a — I understand language constructs for representing structured information. Reads and explains code extracts including those with variables and data structures. Read, build, and test Scratch code that uses the variables y speed, score, lives, and time, together with events, loops, selection, operators, sensing, and broadcasts. You can trace a script and explain how its blocks and variables control movement, scoring, lives, the timer, and game states. TCH 3-15a — I can select appropriate development tools to design, build, evaluate and refine computing solutions based on requirements. Designs and builds a program using a visual language combining constructs and using multiple variables. Use Scratch to design and build a platform game that combines movement, gravity, collision detection, collection, enemy behaviour, scoring, lives, timing, and win/lose conditions. Test each feature and correct problems before adding the next one. Your finished game meets the project requirements, uses several programming constructs and multiple variables, and behaves correctly when tested.

Assessment note

Completing the project can provide evidence towards these benchmarks. You should also be able to explain your code, demonstrate that it meets the requirements, and describe improvements made after testing.

docs.title: Project Updates
docs.text:
Arcade Quest updates

28 August 2026

Floating platforms are now made as a sprite instead of being painted on the backdrop.

  • The ground is part of the backdrop and the boundary script keeps the player at ground level.
  • The floating platforms belong in one Platforms sprite.
  • The player now lands by detecting the Platforms sprite while falling.
  • Platform colour sensing is no longer needed.

If you have already drawn floating platforms on the backdrop, follow Create Platforms in Part 1 to move them into a Platforms sprite, then replace the player code using Add Platform Collision, Check Stage Edges, Move Vertically, Add Gravity, and Jump With Space.

27 August 2026

The instructions and code pictures have been improved after pupil testing.

  • The player now starts safely on screen.
  • Left and right movement now keeps the player upright.
  • Jumping and gravity have been corrected so the player falls back down.
  • Collectables must be separate sprites, not drawings on the backdrop.
  • Completed collectable sprites can be duplicated to make several working collectables.

If you have already started Arcade Quest, check your project against Create Collectables, Set Your Player’s Start Position, Move Left And Right, the Jump And Fall pages, Collect The First Collectable, and Add Collectable Sound before continuing.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Make the character the player will control.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. Open Scratch desktop.
  2. Delete the cat sprite.
  3. Click Choose a Sprite.
  4. Click Paint.
  5. Draw a small arcade player.
  6. Rename the sprite Player.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: Your sprite list should contain a sprite called Player.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Draw the background scenery for your first level.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. Click the Stage and then click Backdrops.
  2. Choose a colour for the sky.
  3. Draw scenery such as clouds, hills, trees or buildings.
  4. Leave space for the player and platforms.

Scenery only

The backdrop can include the ground, but do not add floating platforms or collectables. You will create those as sprites on the next pages.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: The backdrop should contain the sky, scenery and ground, with no floating platforms or collectables painted onto it.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Create the variable that controls jumping and falling.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. In the sprite list below the Stage, click the Player sprite. (If you cannot remember where the sprite list is, go back to Scratch Help: Where To Click Sprites.)
  2. Click Variables.
  3. Click Make a Variable.
  4. Name the variable y speed.
  5. Click OK.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: You should see a variable called y speed.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Make the player move with the arrow keys.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. In the sprite list below the Stage, click the Player sprite. (If you cannot remember where the sprite list is, go back to Scratch Help: Where To Click Sprites.)
  2. Build this code.
  3. Make sure set rotation style says left-right. This stops the player turning upside down.
  4. Press the green flag.
  5. Test the left and right arrow keys.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: The player should move left and right and face the direction it is moving.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Use your custom blocks to make the player fall and land on platforms.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. Click the Player sprite.
  2. Keep your starting-position and left-and-right movement scripts.
  3. Check that you have built collision, check stage edges, and move vertically from the last three tasks.
  4. Build this new script. Find move vertically in My Blocks.

change y speed by -1 makes the player fall. move vertically moves the player and uses your other blocks to check platforms and stage edges.

docs.title: Check
docs.text:
Press the green flag. Drag the player above a platform and release it. It should fall onto the platform and stop.

Try dropping the player where there is no platform. It should stop at ground level, y: -130.

Next: Jump With Space.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Check that every platform works.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. Press the green flag.
  2. Jump onto the ground.
  3. Jump onto each floating platform, then jump again from that platform. Check that the player rises and lands back on it.
  4. Walk off the edge of a platform.
  5. Check that every floating platform belongs to the Platforms sprite if the player falls through one.
  6. Hold space. The player should jump only once.
  7. Try a larger jump-speed value. The player should stop at the top of the Stage.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: The player should land on every floating platform, return to ground level when there is no platform, and remain on the Stage.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Create a separate collectable sprite for the player to grab.

docs.title: Watch First
docs.text: Watch the sprite-making video in Draw Your Player. Then come back to this task.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. Make sure you are looking at the sprite list, not painting the backdrop.
  2. Click Choose a Sprite below the Stage.
  3. Click Paint.
  4. Draw a small coin, gem, star, or piece of fruit.
  5. Rename the new sprite Collectable.
  6. Put it above a platform.

The collectable must be a sprite

Do not paint the collectable onto the backdrop. Backdrop drawings cannot detect the Player, hide, play their own sound, or increase the score.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: Your sprite list should contain separate Player and Collectable sprites.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Create one shared score and make it start at zero each time the game starts.

docs.title: Add The Scoring
docs.text:
1. Click the first Collectable thumbnail in the sprite list below the Stage.
  2. Click Variables, then Make a Variable.
  3. Name the variable score.
  4. Choose For all sprites so every collectable adds to the same score.
  5. Click OK. Tick the box beside score to show the total on the Stage.

docs.title: Reset The Scoring
docs.text:
1. Click the Stage thumbnail beside the sprite list.

  2. Click Code. From Events, drag out when green flag clicked.

  3. From Variables, attach set score to 0. Choose score from the dropdown.

In the next task, the collectable will add points to the shared score.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: You should see score on the Stage. Press the green flag and check that it shows 0.

docs.title: Choose And Save The Collectable's Position
Choose And Save The Collectable's Position
Goal
docs.text: Choose a place for your first collectable and make it return there whenever the game starts.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. Click the Collectable thumbnail below the Stage.

  2. Find the collectable on the Stage—the game screen in the top-right of Scratch. Click and hold the collectable on the game screen, drag it just above a platform, then release the mouse button. Drag the collectable on the Stage, not its thumbnail in the sprite list.

  3. Find the x and y number boxes in the sprite information panel, between the Stage and the sprite list. Write down both numbers.

  4. Click Code.

  5. Click Events and drag when green flag clicked into the code area.

  6. From Motion, attach go to x: y: underneath it. Type your two numbers into it.
  7. From Looks, attach show.

Use your own coordinates. If you already have this script, update it instead of adding another copy.

Keep one collectable for now. Finish its collection code and sound before duplicating it.

docs.title: Check
docs.text:
Drag the collectable to a different place on the Stage, then press the green flag. It should return to your chosen position and be visible.

Keep this script. Next, you will create the shared score and set it to zero. After that, you will add the collection blocks underneath this script.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Make the first collectable add one point and disappear when it touches the player.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
Make sure you have completed Add The Scoring before building the collection code.

  1. Click the first Collectable sprite, then Code.

  2. Attach a forever block below your previous code.

  3. Inside forever, add if then. Put the Sensing touching block into its condition and choose Player from the dropdown.
  4. Inside the if, add Variables change score by 1, then Looks hide, then Control stop this script.

Your one collectable script should now look like this. Keep your own x and y numbers.

change score by 1 adds to the shared total. hide hides this collectable. stop this script stops it adding more points until the game restarts.

docs.title: Check
docs.text:
1. Press the green flag. The score should be 0 and the collectable should appear in its saved place.
  2. Drag Player onto the collectable and release it. You will add keyboard controls in Part 5.
  3. Check that the collectable disappears and the score becomes 1, then stays at 1.
  4. Press the green flag again. The collectable should reappear and the score should reset.

Keep just this first collectable. Add its sound in the next task before duplicating it.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Finish the first collectable by adding a collection sound.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. Click the Collectable sprite.

  2. Click Sounds.

  3. Click Choose a Sound and choose a short sound.

  4. Rename the sound collectable in the sound name box so it matches the code picture.

  5. Click Code. Find the collection script you have already built.
  6. From Sound, drag play sound collectable until done between hide and stop this script.

This is the complete first collectable script. Update your existing script to match; keep your own starting coordinates.

The set score to 0 script stays on the Stage. The collectable only adds points to that shared score.

docs.title: Check Before Duplicating
docs.text:
1. Press the green flag: the collectable appears in its saved position and the score is 0.
  2. Drag Player onto the collectable and release it: the collectable hides, the sound plays, and the score becomes 1.
  3. Wait for the sound to finish: the score must stay at 1.
  4. Press the green flag again: the collectable returns and the score resets.

Once all four checks pass, use Next to duplicate the completed collectable. Its position code, touching check, scoring, and sound will all be copied.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Add something the player should avoid.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. Click Choose a Sprite.
  2. Click Paint.
  3. Draw a simple enemy, like a spike, blob, or robot.
  4. Rename it Enemy.
  5. Put it on a platform the Player can reach.
  6. Make it smaller if it covers most of the platform.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: Your sprite list should contain a sprite called Enemy.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Create the variable that stores how many tries the player has.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. Click Variables.
  2. Click Make a Variable.
  3. Name the variable lives.
  4. Click OK.

Use Make y speed if you need to see the variable buttons again.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: You should see a variable called lives.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Make the game start with three lives.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. In the sprite list below the Stage, click the Player sprite, or click the Stage thumbnail. (If you cannot remember where the sprite list is, go back to Scratch Help: Where To Click Sprites.)
  2. Add a when green flag clicked block.
  3. Add set lives to 3.
  4. Press the green flag.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: The lives variable should show 3.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Make the enemy move back and forth.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. In the sprite list below the Stage, click the Enemy sprite. (If you cannot remember where the sprite list is, go back to Scratch Help: Where To Click Sprites.)
  2. Build this code.
  3. Press the green flag.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: The enemy should move and bounce when it reaches an edge.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Make the enemy send a message when it touches the player.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. In the sprite list below the Stage, click the Enemy sprite. (If you cannot remember where the sprite list is, go back to Scratch Help: Where To Click Sprites.)
  2. Look at the enemy patrol code from Enemy Patrol.
  3. Find the block that says broadcast ouch.
  4. Make sure that block is inside the touching Player check.
  5. Test by touching the enemy.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: The enemy should send the ouch message when the player touches it.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Make the player lose one life after touching an enemy.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. In the sprite list below the Stage, click the Player sprite. (If you cannot remember where the sprite list is, go back to Scratch Help: Where To Click Sprites.)
  2. Build this code.
  3. Test by touching the enemy.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: The player should lose one life and return to the start.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: End the game when the player has no lives left.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. Look at the code from Lose A Life.
  2. Find the if lives = 0 then block.
  3. Make sure it broadcasts game over.
  4. Add when I receive game over to enemies and collectables.
  5. Add hide under that message if you want them to disappear.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: When lives reaches 0, the game should clearly stop or show that it is over.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Add the finish point for the level.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. Click Choose a Sprite.
  2. Click Paint.
  3. Draw a finish flag.
  4. Rename it Flag.
  5. Put it at the far right of the level.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: The player should be able to reach the flag after crossing the level.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Create the variable that stores the timer.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. Click Variables.
  2. Click Make a Variable.
  3. Name the variable time.
  4. Click OK.

Use Make y speed if you need to see the variable buttons again.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: You should see a variable called time.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Make the timer start at 60.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. In the sprite list below the Stage, click the Player sprite, or click the Stage thumbnail. (If you cannot remember where the sprite list is, go back to Scratch Help: Where To Click Sprites.)
  2. Add when green flag clicked.
  3. Add set time to 60.
  4. Press the green flag.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: The time variable should show 60.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Make the timer count down.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. In the sprite list below the Stage, click the Player sprite, or click the Stage thumbnail. (If you cannot remember where the sprite list is, go back to Scratch Help: Where To Click Sprites.)
  2. Build the timer part of this code.
  3. Press the green flag.
  4. Watch the time variable.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: The timer should go down by 1 every second.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Make the player win when they touch the flag.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. In the sprite list below the Stage, click the Player sprite. (If you cannot remember where the sprite list is, go back to Scratch Help: Where To Click Sprites.)
  2. Use the flag part of the code from Count Down.
  3. Make sure it checks touching Flag.
  4. Make it broadcast you win.
  5. Test by moving the player into the flag.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: Touching the flag should send the you win message.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Make the game end when the timer reaches zero.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. In the sprite list below the Stage, click the Player sprite, or click the Stage thumbnail. (If you cannot remember where the sprite list is, go back to Scratch Help: Where To Click Sprites.)
  2. Use the time = 0 part of the code from Count Down.
  3. Make it broadcast game over.
  4. Test by changing the starting time to 5.
  5. Change the starting time back to 60 when it works.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: When time reaches 0, the game should send game over.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Add a simple beginning to the game.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. Create a new backdrop.
  2. Make it a title screen.
  3. Add your game name.
  4. Add a message like Press the green flag.
  5. Switch to the game backdrop when the green flag is clicked.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: The game should have a clear starting screen.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Show the player that they won.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. Create a new backdrop.
  2. Make it a win screen.
  3. Add a message like You Win!.
  4. Add when I receive you win.
  5. Switch to the win backdrop.
  6. Hide enemies and collectables.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: Touching the flag should show the win screen.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Create a new scene for a level that moves sideways.

docs.title: What This Means
docs.text: The Scratch Stage does not really move. Instead, the Player stays near the middle of the screen, and the level sprites move left. In Part 9, you will build this one step at a time.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. Click the Stage thumbnail.
  2. Click Backdrops.
  3. Click Choose a Backdrop.
  4. Click Paint.
  5. Rename the new backdrop Scrolling Level.
  6. Draw the sky and background.
  7. Do not draw platforms on this backdrop.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: You should have a backdrop called Scrolling Level with sky and scenery. Leave platforms off the backdrop so they can move as sprites.

docs.title: Add More Than One Collectable
docs.text:
Only using one collectable?

You can skip this task if your game only has one collectable. Complete it only if you want to add more collectables.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Add more collectables by copying the completed collectable sprite, including its code and sound.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
Once the first collectable has its starting-position code, collection code, and sound, duplicate it to copy everything.

  1. Complete Collect Collectables and Add Collectable Sound on the first Collectable. Test that collecting it adds exactly one point, hides it, and plays its sound before making any copies.
  2. In the sprite list, right-click the Collectable sprite. On a tablet, press and hold it.
  3. Choose duplicate.
  4. Select the new copy and drag it above a different reachable platform.
  5. Read the copy's x and y values below the Stage, then type those numbers into its go to x: y: block. Keep its copied collection code and sound.
  6. Repeat duplicate, move, and update the coordinates for every extra collectable.

Each sprite needs different coordinates. Here are the starting blocks for three example collectables. Change the coordinates at the top of each existing script to give each collectable its own position. Keep the collection loop underneath; do not add another green-flag script:

Use your own x and y numbers—the examples will not fit every level.

Each collectable must be a separate sprite. Do not paint several collectables in one costume or onto the backdrop: Scratch would treat them as one object.

You do not need to write new collection code for each copy. Every collectable runs its own copy of the same script: touching Collectable2 hides only Collectable2, while the other collectables remain available to collect.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: Every collectable should be a separate sprite. Each one should make a sound, add 1 to the score, disappear when collected, and reappear when the green flag is pressed.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Arrange multiple platforms to make a route through the level.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
Keep all your floating platforms in the same costume of the Platforms sprite so the player can detect them together.

  1. Find the sprite list below the Stage (the area where your game appears). Click the thumbnail labelled Platforms.

  2. Look at the sprite information panel between the Stage and the sprite list. Find the number boxes labelled x and y, near the sprite's name.

    The picture shows the player selected. For this task, click Platforms before changing the numbers.

  3. Click inside the x box, select the existing number, type 0, and press Enter.

  4. Click inside the y box, select the existing number, type 0, and press Enter. Both boxes should now show 0. This places the centre of the whole Platforms sprite at the centre of the Stage.

  5. Open Costumes and choose the Select tool.

  6. Select one platform shape and drag it within the costume editor. Watch the Stage to see where it appears in the level.

  7. Move the first platform near the player, a little above ground level.
  8. Move the second platform farther right and a little higher. Leave a gap for jumping.
  9. To add another platform, select a platform shape, copy and paste it, then move the new shape to another position in the same costume.
  10. Leave clear space above each platform for the player and a collectable.

Dragging Platforms on the Stage moves all its platforms together. To move just one platform, select its shape in Costumes. Do not duplicate the whole sprite or create a new costume for each platform.

docs.title: Save The Platforms' Position
docs.text:
Add this code so the whole platform layout returns to the same position when the game starts.

  1. Click the Platforms thumbnail in the sprite list below the Stage.

  2. Click the Code tab.

  3. Click Events. Drag when green flag clicked into the code area.

  4. Click Motion. Drag go to x: y: underneath the green-flag block until they snap together. Enter 0 in both number boxes in this block.
  5. Click Looks. Attach show underneath the go to block.

Your completed script should look like this:

The two zeros match the sprite position you set earlier. The individual platform shapes keep the positions you chose in Costumes.

docs.title: Check
docs.text:
• All floating platforms are shapes in one Platforms costume.
  • The platforms form a route from the player, with gaps for jumping.

To test the starting-position code, drag a platform on the Stage (the game screen). All the platforms should move together. Press the green flag: the whole layout should return to its original position, with x and y both showing 0.

You will test whether the jumps reach each platform in Part 6.

docs.title: Check Your Game World
docs.text:
Before starting Part 2, check that you have:

  • A backdrop with sky, scenery, and ground.
  • A Player sprite.
  • A Platforms sprite with the floating platforms drawn in one costume.
  • A Collectable sprite.

Compare your project with this example. Your artwork can be different. You will arrange the sprites and add their code in the next parts.

Use Next at the bottom of the page to start Part 2.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Make a block that keeps the player between the top and bottom of the Stage.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
Select the Player sprite.

  1. Click My Blocks → Make a Block.
  2. Name it check stage edges.
  3. Tick Run without screen refresh.
  4. Click OK.
  5. Build the script below.

The first check stops the player at the top of the Stage. The second stops them at ground level. set on ground to 1 lets the player jump after landing on the ground.

docs.title: Check
docs.text:
Check the numbers: 170 for the top and -130 for the bottom.

Keep your collision block. We will connect both blocks on the next page.

Next: Move Vertically.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Create an object for the player to collect.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. Click Choose a Sprite below the Stage.
  2. Click Paint.
  3. Draw a small coin, gem, star or piece of fruit.
  4. Rename the sprite Collectable.
  5. Put it above a platform.

Use a sprite

Do not paint the collectable on the backdrop. A separate sprite can detect the player, increase the score, play a sound and disappear.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Create the floating platforms as one sprite.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. Click Choose a Sprite.
  2. Click Paint.
  3. Rename the sprite Platforms.
  4. Draw one floating platform.
  5. Without adding another costume, draw a second floating platform in a different position.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: The sprite list should contain a Platforms sprite with two floating platforms in its costume.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Move in small steps so the player cannot skip through a thin platform.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
Select the Player sprite.

  1. Click My Blocks → Make a Block.
  2. Name it move vertically.
  3. Tick Run without screen refresh, then click OK.
  4. Build the script below. Use the pink blocks you made on the last two pages.
  5. For abs of, use the green Operators block with the dropdown and select abs.

abs gives the number of steps. For example, a speed of -5 means five steps down. The block checks for a collision after each step.

docs.title: Check
docs.text:
Check that both directions call collision and check stage edges after moving one pixel.

Your three custom blocks are ready. On the next page, you will build the gravity script that runs them.

Next: Add Gravity.

docs.title: Check Your Game World
docs.text:
Before starting Part 5, check that your sprite list contains separate Player, Platforms and Collectable sprites.

Check that the player is on the left, the platforms form a route, and the first collectable is above a platform. Press the green flag to check that the platforms and collectable return to their saved positions.

Drag the Player onto each collectable and release it. Each collectable should add one point, disappear, and play its sound. Press the green flag again: the score should reset to 0 and all collectables should reappear. You will add movement in Part 5 and jumping in Part 6.

When you are ready, use Next at the bottom of the page to start Part 5.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Stop the player falling through platforms.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
Select the Player sprite. Create a variable named on ground for this sprite only. Use 1 for standing on a platform or the ground, and 0 for being in the air.

Then follow these steps.

  1. Click My Blocks.
  2. Click Make a Block.
  3. Name it collision.
  4. Tick Run without screen refresh.
  5. Click OK.
  6. Put this code under define collision.

In each touching block, choose the sprite containing your platforms.

docs.title: Check
docs.text:
Your collision definition should match the picture. Check that each touching block uses your platform sprite.

We will use this block in Move Vertically, then run it when we build Add Gravity.

Next: Check Stage Edges.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Make the platforms, collectables, enemy, and flag move using scroll x.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
Build this code on Platform 1.

  1. In the sprite list below the Stage, click Platform 1. (If you cannot remember where the sprite list is, go back to Scratch Help: Where To Click Sprites.)
  2. Build this code.

docs.title: Change The Number
docs.text:
The code image uses 0.

For each sprite, change the 0 to the number below:

  • Platform 1: use 0
  • Platform 2: use 240
  • Platform 3: use 480
  • Collectable: use 300
  • Enemy: use 520
  • Flag: use 700

Build the same code on Platform 2, Platform 3, Collectable, Enemy, and Flag.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: Each level sprite should have scrolling code with its own starting-position number. Press the arrow keys and check that the sprites move together.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Use the arrow keys to change the scrolling position.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. In the sprite list below the Stage, click the Player sprite.
  2. Build this code.
  3. Add switch backdrop to Scrolling Level under the green flag block.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: Press the green flag. The Scrolling Level backdrop should appear and scroll x should reset to 0. Press the arrow keys and check that scroll x changes. You will connect the level sprites to this variable in the next task.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Check that the player looks like they are travelling through a longer level.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. Press the green flag.
  2. Hold the right arrow key. Check that the platforms, collectables, enemy, and flag move left.
  3. Hold the left arrow key and check that the level moves the other way.
  4. Press the green flag again and check that the scrolling position resets.

docs.title: Check
docs.text:
• The level sprites move together as the player travels.
  • The player looks like they are moving through a longer level.
  • Restarting the game resets the scrolling position.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Create a variable to track how far the level has scrolled.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. Click Variables.
  2. Click Make a Variable.
  3. Name the variable scroll x.
  4. Choose For all sprites so the player and level sprites can use the same value.
  5. Click OK.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: Select the Player and then Platform 1. The same scroll x variable should be available on both sprites.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Make three platform sprites that can move across the scrolling scene.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. Click Choose a Sprite.
  2. Click Paint.
  3. Draw one green rectangle platform.
  4. Rename it Platform 1.
  5. Right-click Platform 1.
  6. Click duplicate.
  7. Rename the copy Platform 2.
  8. Right-click Platform 2.
  9. Click duplicate.
  10. Rename the copy Platform 3.
  11. Put the three platforms across the new scene.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: Your sprite list should contain Platform 1, Platform 2, and Platform 3. Each platform should be a separate sprite.

docs.title: Part 2: Set Your Player's Start Position
Goal
docs.text: Set up the player's starting position and direction.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
This is the first coding step for your Player sprite.

  1. Click the Player sprite in the sprite list below the Stage.
  2. Check that the player is small enough to fit on your platforms. Adjust Size below the Stage if needed.
  3. Build this code to place the player on the left at the start of the game.

When you click the green flag, the player starts at x: -180, y: -130 and faces right.

Keep this script on the sprite as you add movement and jumping in the next steps.

In Check Stage Edges, you will make a block that stops the player at ground level.

docs.title: Check
docs.text:
1. Press the green flag. The player should appear at the left of the Stage, facing right.
  2. Move the player somewhere else, then press the green flag again. It should return to x: -180, y: -130.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Make the player jump from the ground or a platform, once for each press of the space bar.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. Click the Player sprite.
  2. Build the script below.
  3. Keep the starting-position and movement scripts, plus the gravity script and all three custom blocks from the previous tasks. Do not add a separate collision loop.
  4. Use on ground from Add Platform Collision to allow a jump only while standing on a platform or the ground. Set it to 0 immediately when jumping.
  5. Press the green flag, then tap space.

docs.title: Check
docs.text:
• The player jumps when you press space.
  • Holding space does not keep starting new jumps.
  • Releasing space lets you press it again for another jump after landing.
  • Press space repeatedly while in the air. It must not restart the jump.
  • Jump underneath a platform. The player should hit its underside and fall back down.
  • Land on a platform, release space, then press it again. The player should jump up from the platform without falling through it.
  • The player falls back down and stops on a platform or at ground level.

docs.title: Scratch Boat Race
docs.text: Build a boat-racing game where you steer with the mouse, avoid wooden barriers, use boosters, and reach an island as quickly as possible.

docs.title: Get Started
docs.text:
1. Open Scratch desktop.
  2. Use Next at the bottom of this page to open Open The Starter Project.
  3. Download and open the starter file, then build and test your game one task at a time.

Work at your own pace

The project has six parts, followed by optional challenges. A part may take more than one class session. Complete and check each task before moving on. If you have already started, carry on from your last task using the navigation.

docs.title: Experiences and Outcomes
docs.text:
Experience and Outcome What you will do in Boat Race Evidence of success TCH 3-13a — Information processes and how they communicate Run the boat, Stage timer, and spinning gate scripts at the same time. Explore how stop all ends them together. You can identify the separate processes and explain what happens to them when the player wins. TCH 3-14a — Read and explain programming constructs Build and trace scripts using events, loops, conditions, sensing, operators, and the time variable. You can explain how the code controls movement, crashes, boosters, and timing. TCH 3-15a — Design, build, evaluate, and refine a solution Build the race from a starter project, test each feature, fix problems, and add an improvement. Your game meets its requirements, and you can describe a change made after testing.

Assessment note

This project can contribute evidence towards these outcomes. It uses one variable, time; further work with multiple variables is needed to demonstrate that aspect of the Level 3 design-and-build benchmark. Be ready to explain your code and demonstrate your testing.

docs.title: Need Something Else?
docs.text:
• Scratch Help: find sprites, read code images, and choose colours.
  • Project Updates: find your place if you started the earlier six-step guide.

docs.text:

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Choose one or more challenges to improve your Boat Race game.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. Save your working game before changing it.
  2. Choose a challenge below and build one improvement at a time.
  3. Test your change, then repeat the finished game checks.

docs.title: Add sound effects
docs.text:
You could add sound effects that play when:

  • The boat crashes.
  • The boat reaches the island.
  • The boat touches the wooden barrier.
  • The timer starts.
How to add a sound

Option 1: add a sound from Scratch:

  1. Click the sprite or the Stage where you want the sound to play.
  2. Click the Sounds tab.
  3. Click Choose a Sound.
  4. Search for a sound effect, for example pop, splash, or cheer.
  5. Click the sound to add it to your project.
  6. Go back to the Code tab.
  7. Add a sound block where you want the sound to play.

Option 2: upload a sound effect to Scratch:

  1. Go to Pixabay Sound Effects.
  2. Search for a sound effect that matches your game.
  3. Download the sound file.
  4. Go back to Scratch.
  5. Click the sprite or the Stage where you want the sound to play.
  6. Click the Sounds tab.
  7. Click Upload Sound.
  8. Choose the sound file you downloaded.
  9. Go back to the Code tab.
  10. Add a sound block where you want the sound to play.

docs.title: Add background music
docs.text:
You could also add background music to make your game feel more complete.

How to find and add royalty-free music

You can find royalty-free music on Pixabay Music.

To add music to your Scratch project:

  1. Go to Pixabay Music.
  2. Search for a short piece of music that matches your game, for example arcade, race, or adventure.
  3. Preview the track before downloading it.
  4. Download the music file.
  5. Go back to Scratch.
  6. Click the Stage.
  7. Click the Sounds tab.
  8. Click Upload Sound.
  9. Choose the music file you downloaded.
  10. Add code to the Stage to play the music.

Example:

If the music is too loud, use the sound editor in Scratch to make it quieter.

docs.title: Add another player
docs.text:
You could turn your game into a race between two players. Player 1 can keep using the mouse. Player 2 can use the keyboard.

How to add a second player

To add a second player:

  1. Right-click the boat sprite.
  2. Choose Duplicate.
  3. Rename the new sprite Player 2.
  4. Change the colour or costume so it is easy to tell the two boats apart.
  5. Move Player 2 to a different starting position.
  6. Add keyboard controls to Player 2.

Player 2 could use:

  • Up arrow to move forward.
  • Left arrow to turn left.
  • Right arrow to turn right.

Example:

Remember to add crash and winning code for Player 2 as well.

docs.title: More ideas
docs.text:
You could also:

  • Add more obstacles to your game.
  • Add green slime to your backdrop and make the slime slow the boat down.
  • Add a moving obstacle, for example, a log or a shark.
  • Create more levels by adding different backdrops.
  • Let the player choose which level to play.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: Your improvement works and the original race still plays correctly. Save your project and explain what you changed and how you tested it.

docs.title: How To Use The Code Images
docs.text:
Copy the blocks into Scratch one at a time. When an image shows a script you have already started, update that script. Keep the blocks from earlier tasks unless the instructions tell you to change them. Outlined sections show the new code to add.

Click a code image to enlarge it if the block text is difficult to read.

docs.title: Where To Click Sprites
docs.text: The sprite list is below the Stage. Click the boat thumbnail to edit the boat, or the gate thumbnail to edit the gate. Click the Stage thumbnail beside the sprite list to work on the timer or backdrops.

docs.title: Choose A Colour From The Stage
docs.text:
1. Click the colour input in the touching color block.
  2. Click the eyedropper at the bottom of the colour picker.
  3. Move over the Stage and click the colour you need: brown wood, yellow island, or white booster.
  4. Click in the Code area to close the picker.

Earlier page Continue here Step 1: Get Started Open The Starter Project Step 2: Control The Boat Follow The Mouse Step 3: Add Crashes Make A Hit Costume Step 4: Reach The Island Add The Winning Condition Step 5: Add A Timer Make time Step 6: Obstacles And Boosters Draw Booster Arrows

The original step links still open a list of the corresponding tasks. The challenges remain available after the final check.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
Open and save your own copy of Boat Race.

Download the Boat Race starter project

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. Download the starter project using the button above.
  2. Open Scratch desktop.
  3. Choose File → Load from your computer.
  4. Open your Downloads folder, select BoatRace.sb3, and click Open.
  5. Choose File → Save to your computer and save your copy somewhere you can find it again.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: The project opens with a boat and a race course. You have saved your own copy.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Find the boat, barriers, and finish before adding code.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. Look at the Stage. Find the water, brown wooden barriers, and yellow island.
  2. Find the boat in the sprite list below the Stage. Click its thumbnail.
  3. Click Code. This is where you will build the boat’s movement script.
  4. Plan a route from the bottom left of the course to the island without crossing the wood.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: You can point to the boat, explain what it must avoid, and show where it must finish.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Make the boat start in the bottom left and follow the mouse.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. In the sprite list below the Stage, click the boat. Click Code.
  2. Build the script in the image. Set the starting direction to 0 and the starting position to x: -190, y: -150.
  3. Put point towards mouse-pointer and move 1 steps inside the forever loop.
  4. Press the green flag and move the mouse around the water on the Stage.
  5. Hold the mouse still and watch what happens when the boat reaches it.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: The boat follows the pointer. It may wobble when it reaches the pointer; you will fix that in the next task.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Stop the boat moving when it is close to the mouse.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. Select the boat and find the movement script you just built.
  2. Inside forever, wrap the two movement blocks in an if then block from Control.
  3. From Operators, put a > block into the condition.
  4. Put distance to mouse-pointer from Sensing on the left and 5 on the right.
  5. Compare your updated script with the image. Update the existing script rather than building a second copy.
  6. Press the green flag. Move the pointer, then hold it still.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: The boat follows the mouse and settles when it gets close. Explain why the movement blocks only run when the distance is greater than 5.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Give the boat a second costume to show a crash.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. Select the boat and open the Costumes tab.
  2. Rename the original boat costume normal.
  3. Right-click its costume thumbnail and choose duplicate.
  4. Rename the copy hit.
  5. With hit selected, use the Select tool to move and rotate pieces so the boat looks broken. Keep the normal costume intact.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: The boat has two costumes named exactly normal and hit. Click each thumbnail to check the difference.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Make the boat crash and return to the start when it touches wood.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. Select the boat and click Code.
  2. Add another if then inside the existing forever, below the mouse movement condition. Do not put it inside the distance check.
  3. Use touching color from Sensing as the condition. Use the eyedropper to select brown from a wooden barrier.
  4. Inside this new condition, add the costume, speech, direction, and position blocks shown in the outlined section of the image.
  5. Set the reset position to x: -190, y: -150 and direction to 0.
  6. Press the green flag and steer into a wooden barrier.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: The boat switches to hit, shows a crash message for two seconds, then changes back to normal and returns to the start.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Make every new race start with an undamaged boat.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. Select the boat and find the top of its movement script.
  2. Add switch costume to normal directly below when green flag clicked, before the direction and position blocks.
  3. Keep all the movement and crash code below these starting blocks.
  4. Open Costumes and select hit, then press the green flag.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: The boat immediately changes to normal and starts from the bottom left, even if it was showing the hit costume before the race.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: End the race when the boat reaches the island.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. Select the boat and find its forever loop.
  2. Add a new if then below the crash condition, still inside forever.
  3. Put touching color in the condition. Use the eyedropper to select yellow from the island.
  4. Inside this condition, add say YEAH! for 2 seconds, then stop all.
  5. Check the dropdown on the stop block says all.
  6. Compare your script with the image and sail to the island.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: The boat says YEAH! for two seconds and then all scripts stop. The mouse no longer moves the boat.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Check movement, crashes, winning, and restarting together.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. Press the green flag. Check that the boat starts at x: -190, y: -150.
  2. Move the mouse, then hold it still. Check that the boat follows and settles near the pointer.
  3. Touch a barrier. Check that the boat changes costume and returns to the start.
  4. Reach the island. If testing is difficult, temporarily change only the first go to block to place the boat near the island, as shown below.
  5. After testing, restore the first go to block to x: -190, y: -150. Leave the crash reset at the same starting position.
  6. Press the green flag again and check that a new race begins. Save your project.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: All four behaviours work: following, crashing, winning, and restarting. Fix any failed check before adding the timer.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Create a variable to display how long the race takes.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. Click the Stage thumbnail beside the sprite list, then click Code.
  2. Click Variables, then Make a Variable.
  3. Name it time. Create it for all sprites if Scratch offers that choice.
  4. Click OK and tick the box beside time to show it on the Stage.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: A variable named time is visible on the Stage. It does not count yet; you will add that code next.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Reset the timer for each race and count in tenths of a second.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. Select the Stage and click Code.
  2. Build the script in the image. Put set time to 0 immediately below when green flag clicked.
  3. Add a forever loop with wait 0.1 seconds followed by change time by 0.1.
  4. Press the green flag and watch time increase while you steer.
  5. Crash into a barrier. The timer should keep counting while the boat returns to the start.
  6. Reach the island. The timer stops when stop all runs, after the two-second winning message.
  7. Press the green flag again to check that time resets. Save your project.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: The timer starts at zero, counts during the race, and stops when the game ends. You can explain how the Stage’s timer and the boat’s movement run at the same time.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Add white areas to the course where the boat will speed up.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. Select the Stage and open Backdrops.
  2. Select the race course backdrop you are using.
  3. Use the paint tools to draw white arrows on the water, like the example.
  4. Keep a clear route past the wooden barriers and towards the island.
  5. Return to Code.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: White booster arrows appear on the race course. They will change the boat’s speed after the next task.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Make the boat move three extra steps when it touches a booster.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. Select the boat and find its existing forever loop.
  2. Add the if then block shown below at the bottom of that loop, outside the other conditions. Keep the movement, crash, and win conditions.
  3. Use touching color and the eyedropper to select white from an arrow.
  4. Put move 3 steps inside this condition.
  5. Press the green flag and steer across an arrow, then back onto the water.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: The boat moves faster while touching white and returns to its usual speed on the water.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Create a wooden gate for the boat to avoid.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. Open Choose a Sprite, select Paint, and rename the new sprite gate.
  2. Draw a long, narrow rectangle in the same brown as the wooden barriers. Use colour 9, saturation 100, and brightness 40 to match the starter course.
  3. Position the costume so the centre marker is in the middle of the rectangle. This is the point it will rotate around.
  4. Place the gate across part of the water. Resize it if necessary, leaving enough room for the boat to get past.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: A sprite called gate appears on the course. Its costume is centred and matches the wooden barriers.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Make the wooden gate turn continuously during the race.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. Select gate in the sprite list and click Code.
  2. Build the script in the image: when green flag clicked, then forever containing turn 1 degrees.
  3. Press the green flag. Check that the gate turns around its centre.
  4. Steer the boat into the gate. Your existing brown colour check should trigger a crash.
  5. Sail past the gate to the island and check that the gate stops when the game ends.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: The gate spins during play, touching it causes a crash, and winning stops it. If contact does not cause a crash, check that its brown matches the barriers.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Test the complete game and explain how your code works.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
1. Press the green flag and check the boat’s position, normal costume, and timer reset.
  2. Follow the mouse across water and stop near the pointer.
  3. Touch a barrier and then the gate. Both should cause a crash and reset the boat.
  4. Cross a booster and check that the boat speeds up.
  5. Reach the island. After the winning message, the boat, timer, and gate should stop.
  6. Restart and complete another race. Save your project.
  7. Explain one loop, one condition, and the time variable to a partner. Describe one problem you found and how you fixed it.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: Every feature works together. You can demonstrate your game, explain its code, and describe an improvement made after testing.
